transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi, doctor. Thank you. I just... I really didn't know where else to go at this point. What brings me in is that I just keep getting hit, completely out of nowhere, with this... this scene of my cousin on that pavement. It's like my brain just hijacks me. I'll be right back there, and I can hear all the shouting, the chaotic yelling from that night, and I see the lights flashing all over again. And it's so real, you know? It's not just remembering it, it's like I'm living it. 

It happens at the worst times, too. I'll just be standing there in the church office—I work in ministry, so I'm supposed to be the one holding it together for everyone else, being the steady one—and I'll be trying so hard to just act normal, to smile and do my job and be present for my congregation, but inside I'm just completely overwhelmed by the sights and sounds of that street. It just won't stop playing in my head. I can't keep pretending I'm fine when I'm constantly getting pulled back to that pavement, no matter how hard I try to just focus on my work.
Do you find yourself avoiding certain places, people, or activities because they remind you of that night?

Yeah, I... I do. Constantly, actually. It dictates my whole schedule now, to be honest. Like, just getting to the church every morning has turned into this massive ordeal. I used to just take the main road, which is a straight shot and goes right past the community center and that court. But now, I take the long way around town. I will literally drive miles out of my way, winding through all these random back residential neighborhoods and dealing with all the school zone traffic, just so I don't have to pass by the community center or that court. I can't even look in that general direction without feeling like I'm going to completely fall apart right there in the driver's seat. 

And it is not just the driving, either. It is the talking. People at the church, they mean well, you know? They really do. They want to check in on me, or they want to talk about what happened because it shook up the whole community and they think talking about it is healing. But if somebody starts talking about that night, I just... I can't handle it. I shut it down completely. I know I am a minister and my entire vocation is supposed to be about listening and processing grief with people, but I just find a reason to leave. I will pretend I have an urgent phone call, or I will say I left my sermon notes in my office, or I will just walk away almost mid-sentence if I have to. I feel terrible about it later, being so dismissive to my congregation, but I just cannot let them talk about it. The second they do, I am right back there.
Do you have trouble sleeping at night?

Actually... no. Not really. I mean, you would probably think so, right? Given everything I just told you about how my brain won't shut off during the day and how I'm constantly on edge. A lot of folks in my congregation, when they go through a sudden loss or a really hard season, the first thing they tell me is that their sleep is completely wrecked. I actually have this whole file of pastoral care resources in my office specifically about finding rest and peace at night because it's such a common issue. 

But for me... I think I am just so entirely depleted by the time the day is over. Like, physically and emotionally drained from just trying to hold up this mask for everyone else. By the time I get back to my apartment—and my days are long, you know, sometimes I'm at the church from 8 AM until 9 or 10 at night if we have a youth group event or a deacons meeting—I am just running on absolute empty. I'll get home, I'll try to do my evening prayers, maybe read a few pages of a theological commentary I'm studying for my Sunday sermon, and the second my head hits the pillow, my body just completely shuts down. 

It's almost like a defense mechanism, I think. I just crash. I sleep really heavy, actually, straight through till my alarm goes off. It is honestly the only time my brain goes quiet and I get a break from the flashing lights and the yelling. So, no, I haven't had any trouble sleeping. The nights aren't the problem for me... it's the waking hours that are the nightmare. If I couldn't sleep on top of having to dodge half the town and pretend I'm fine all day, I honestly don't know how I would even be functioning right now.
Do you often feel irritable or have outbursts of anger?

I... yeah. Yes, I do. And it's... it's really starting to scare me, honestly, because it is so entirely out of character for me. I mean, my whole calling, my whole life's work, is about patience and grace, you know? I'm supposed to be the one who diffuses tension, the peacemaker. I went to seminary for four years learning how to shepherd people through conflict, how to listen with empathy, how to turn the other cheek. And I used to be so good at it. I really was. People would come to me because I was calm, because I was the safe harbor when things got heated.

But lately... it's like my fuse is just completely gone. It's like it burned away the night my cousin died, and now there's just a raw wire right under my skin. Just last week, we had our monthly deacons meeting. And it's usually just mundane stuff—budget approvals, planning the church picnic, scheduling volunteers for the food pantry. Normal, boring church business. And one of the older deacons, a man I have known and respected since I started this job, he just asked a simple question about the youth group budget. He wasn't being malicious or critical, he just asked if we could maybe trim a few dollars from the pizza fund. 

And doctor, I just... I snapped. I completely lost it. It wasn't just a mild disagreement; I raised my voice. I was practically yelling at him, right there in the fellowship hall in front of everyone. I was talking to him like he was the enemy, like he was actively trying to sabotage the entire ministry, over fifty dollars in pizza money. I could see the shock on everyone's faces. The room went dead silent. And it's not just the deacons, either. I've been doing it with the youth leaders too, the volunteers who give up their Wednesday nights to help me. If they are five minutes late, or if they forget to print the discussion questions, I just lash out. 

And the worst part... the absolute worst part is how I feel afterward. The second the words are out of my mouth, the second I see them shrink back, I just feel this crushing wave of guilt. I hate it. I hate how fast I go from zero to absolute rage. I hate that I'm hurting the people who are trying to support me, the people I'm supposed to be leading. I'll go back to my office and just put my head on my desk and think, 'Who am I becoming?' It's like I have all this jagged, chaotic energy trapped inside me from that pavement, and it just explodes out of me at the people who least deserve it. I have to spend half my week apologizing for things I said in the heat of the moment, and I just... I don't know how to stop it from happening. It's like I'm not even in control of my own reactions anymore.
Do you ever feel like you're outside of your body, watching yourself, when these memories or emotions overwhelm you?

Outside my body... no. No, I don't think I've ever felt that. Honestly, it's almost the exact opposite for me. If anything, I feel entirely too trapped inside my body when it happens, if that makes sense. 

I know some people talk about feeling like they're floating or like they're watching a movie of their own life when things get to be too much... we actually touched on that a little bit in some of my pastoral counseling courses in undergrad, how the mind sometimes tries to protect itself by just detaching from reality when the pain is too heavy. And to be completely honest with you, Doctor, there are times when I almost wish my brain would do that. I wish I could just check out and watch from the ceiling for a few minutes just to get a break from the sheer intensity of it all. 

But for me, when the memories come crashing in, or when I get so overwhelmed by the grief and the panic that I can barely breathe, I am painfully aware of my physical body. I feel every single thing. My chest gets incredibly tight, my hands start sweating, my heart feels like it's going to hammer right through my ribs. I'm not watching myself from above; I'm right there, anchored to the ground, feeling like the weight of the entire sanctuary is pressing down on my shoulders. 

Like, just the other day, I was standing in the church foyer talking to one of our elderly members about the Sunday flower arrangements, and I heard a car backfire out on the main street. And instantly, I wasn't floating away. I was right back on that pavement. I could practically feel the cold concrete under my knees again, I could smell the exhaust in the air. I gripped the edge of the wooden welcome table so hard my knuckles went completely white, just trying to stay upright and keep my balance. I was so hyper-aware of my own physical panic, just praying she wouldn't notice that my hands were shaking and I was struggling to pull air into my lungs. So, no... I don't ever get that feeling of watching myself from the outside. I am stuck right inside every single agonizing second of it, and it feels like there is absolutely no escape.
Do you try to push away or avoid thoughts and memories of that night when they come to mind?

Oh, absolutely. I mean, it is practically a full-time job at this point just trying to keep it all at bay. I do everything in my human power to avoid... well, anything that even remotely points back to it. 

Like, physically, for one. I actually take the long way around town now everywhere I go, just so I don't have to pass the community center or that court. It adds probably fifteen or twenty minutes to my drive, depending on the time of day, which I know sounds completely ridiculous because it’s really not a huge town, but I just... I can't look at it. If I even get close to that intersection, I start panicking, so I just map out these elaborate, winding detours through the residential neighborhoods to completely bypass that whole side of town. Even if I'm running late for a staff meeting, I will take the detour. I just can't go near there.

And it's not just the places, it's the conversations, too. You know, in my line of work, people want to talk. They want to process grief, they want to make sense of tragedy, they want to find the theology in it... so they bring it up. They’ll come up to me after Sunday service, or during coffee hour, or even just running into them at the grocery store, and they’ll start saying, 'Pastor, I was just thinking about that awful night...' or they'll bring up my cousin. And the second—the absolute second—I realize where the sentence is going, I just shut it down. I have to. 

I'll pivot the conversation to something entirely different, like the upcoming church picnic or the youth retreat, or if I can't do that, I'll just find a reason to leave. I'll pretend my phone is vibrating in my pocket, or I'll say I need to go check on the audio-visual team in the sound booth, or that I left my sermon notes on the printer. I know it probably comes across as rude, or dismissive, which goes against everything I was taught in pastoral care about being present with people in their pain. But if I let them pull me into a conversation about that night... if I actually let myself sit there and think about it and picture it again... I’ll just completely unravel right there in the fellowship hall. So I just spend my whole day dodging it. I push the thoughts away, I change my driving routes, I cut people off... I'm just constantly running in the opposite direction so I don't have to face it.
Do you often feel guilty or ashamed about something related to that night?

Yeah. Yeah, I do. Honestly, it's... it's not even just sometimes. It is every single day. Most days, I wake up, and before I even open my eyes, before I even look at the alarm clock or think about what I have to do at the church that day, I just feel it. It’s this massive, suffocating mix of fear, anger, and just profound guilt, and it just sits right there in the center of my chest. It feels like a physical weight that I can't breathe under. 

And the shame... the shame is just unbearable, because I look at what happened, and I just feel like I completely failed everyone. I feel like I failed God, for one. I'm a youth pastor, I'm supposed to have this unwavering faith and trust in His providence, but I'm just so angry and terrified all the time, and I feel like a massive hypocrite every time I bow my head to pray. And my family... I failed my family. I failed my cousin. I was right there, and I couldn't save him. I couldn't stop it. 

And then I have to go into work and look at the kids in my youth group... these teenagers who look up to me, who trusted me to be a leader, to keep them safe, to have the answers. And I just feel like I failed them, too. How can they trust me? How can anyone trust me? I just walk around all day with this awful, heavy cocktail of negative emotions sitting on my chest, from the absolute second I wake up until I finally manage to pass out at night, just obsessing over how I let God down, I let my family down, and I let those kids down. I just... I can't shake it. I try to pray it away, I try to read scripture, I try to busy myself with sermon prep, but the guilt is just always, always there, telling me I didn't do enough.
Do you believe you're a bad person because of what happened that night?

A bad person? ...No. No, I don't think I would say that. I mean, I know I just went on and on about the guilt and the shame, and feeling like a massive failure, but... there is a difference, I think, between failing and being fundamentally bad. I don't believe I'm a bad person. 

I mean, if I look at my life and my calling to ministry, I went into this because I genuinely want to help people. I love the teenagers in my youth group. I loved my cousin. My intentions have never been malicious. I never wanted anyone to get hurt, ever. So, when I really sit down and examine my heart—which is something we’re taught to do constantly in seminary, just this rigorous spiritual self-examination—I don't find evil there. I don't look in the mirror and see a monster or a villain. 

Actually, I was just reading a commentary on Peter’s denial of Christ the other day for a devotional I’m trying to write, and I was thinking about how Peter wasn't a *bad* person. He was just terrified. He failed in a moment of sheer, overwhelming panic. And honestly, that’s kind of how I view myself right now. I don't think I'm bad; I just think I was weak. I feel like a coward, maybe, or just incredibly inadequate. 

I don't want it to sound like I'm letting myself off the hook by saying that, because believe me, Doctor, I am not. Like I said, the guilt is practically eating me alive every hour of the day. But if you're asking if I have this core belief that I am just a rotten, terrible human being because of what happened... no. I just see a guy who wasn't strong enough, or fast enough, or brave enough when it actually mattered. I think there's a pretty significant distinction there, both theologically and just... personally. So, no, I don't think I'm a bad person. Just a deeply flawed one who couldn't do what needed to be done.
Have you ever felt like you're in a daze or spaced out when thinking about that night?

Spaced out? Um... no. No, I wouldn't say that. I think I know what you mean, like when people just sort of check out or their mind goes completely blank and they just stare at the wall? I don't really get like that. If anything, it’s the exact opposite for me. When I think about that night, or when a memory tries to force its way in, I don't go numb or get into a daze at all. I get... well, like I was saying earlier, I just panic. Everything gets incredibly sharp, and my heart starts hammering, and I'm just painfully, acutely aware of everything. 

I mean, honestly, Doctor, there are days when I think it would almost be a relief to just... space out. To just have my brain hit a pause button and turn to static for a few minutes so I wouldn't have to feel the weight of it all. But my mind just doesn't do that. It doesn't give me that kind of break. Instead, I'm just constantly on high alert, trying to dodge the thoughts. 

Like just the other day, I was in the church office trying to organize the permission slips for the upcoming youth lock-in, and someone slammed a heavy door out in the hallway, and my mind immediately wanted to go back to that night. But I didn't zone out. I just instantly felt that massive wave of guilt and fear I was telling you about, and I had to physically get up and pace around the fellowship hall just to keep myself moving and keep the thoughts away. So, no, no daze. No spacing out. It's all just very... very raw and very present. Almost too present, if you know what I mean. I never really lose touch with where I am, I just... I just want to escape what I'm feeling.
Do you ever feel like you're disconnected from yourself or the world around you when you're not having one of these flashbacks?

Disconnected? Like... like from my own body, or feeling like things aren't real? No. No, I don't think so. Honestly, it goes right back to what I was just saying about not spacing out. I am just... I am so painfully tethered to myself and to the world right now. 

I feel every single second of the day. There's no detachment at all. If anything, the world feels almost too loud, too bright, too... present, I guess? Like, when I'm standing in the sanctuary on Sunday mornings, or even just sitting in the local coffee shop trying to read through my emails and prep for Wednesday night youth group, I don't feel like I'm floating away or like my surroundings are fake. I know exactly who I am, I know exactly where I am, and I am acutely aware of exactly what I failed to do. 

It's like I'm hyper-connected to my own skin, and it's just constantly buzzing with all this tension. I look at the people around me—the congregation, the kids, the senior pastor—and they all feel very, very real. The conversations we have are real. I might feel like there's this invisible barrier between me and them sometimes, but that's not because I'm disconnected from reality. It's just because I'm carrying this massive, suffocating weight of guilt that they don't see or fully understand. But I am definitely, one hundred percent in my own body. 

I feel every physical ache, every time my stomach ties itself into knots—which is basically constantly these days. I mean, I've even had a few of the older congregants pull me aside after service to ask if I'm feeling alright because they say I look so tense and rigid all the time. So I know I'm physically reacting to the world around me. I'm not floating above it or checking out of it. I'm just dragging myself through it, inch by inch. I really, really wish I could feel disconnected sometimes, Doctor. I honestly do. Just to get a five-minute breather from being me, from feeling all this shame. But my brain just won't let me off the hook like that. I'm just stuck right here in the thick of it, completely grounded in how awful I feel, every single minute of the day.
Have you lost interest in things you used to enjoy doing?

Yeah... yeah, I really have. Honestly, it's been one of the hardest things to hide from everyone at the church. Because... well, I used to just have so much passion for things. I used to absolutely love preaching, you know? Getting up there, opening up a text, really connecting with the youth group... it was my calling, it fueled me. But now, I just stand up there and I'm totally just going through the motions. I'm just reading words off a page. 

And it's not just the heavy ministry stuff, either. It's everything. I play keys—or, well, I used to play keys for the worship band sometimes, and I'd get so lost in the music, just really feeling the joy of it. Now, if I sit at the keyboard, my hands just feel like lead. I don't feel anything. 

It's the same with my hobbies outside the church. I used to love taking pictures. I'd take my camera everywhere with me, trying to capture these great, vibrant moments of life, just looking for beauty in things. But I haven't even taken the lens cap off in... I don't even know how long. And even just physical stuff, like running with the guys on the court. We had this Tuesday night pickup basketball game, just some guys from the young adult ministry and the neighborhood. I used to look forward to it all week. The energy, the camaraderie, just sweating it out... but the last couple times I tried to go, I just felt completely hollow. I couldn't get into it, and now I just avoid it altogether. I just make up excuses about having too much paperwork or needing to study. 

It's just... I don't know how else to describe it, Doctor, except that none of it feels alive in me anymore. All those things that used to bring me joy or make me feel like *me*, they're just... flat. The spark is completely burnt out. So I just do the bare minimum, going through the motions to keep people from asking too many questions, but inside... yeah, there's just no interest left. None of it reaches me anymore.
Do you blame yourself for what happened that night?

Do I blame myself? I mean... how could I not? Honestly, Doctor, that is... that is the absolute core of it all. It’s what I wake up thinking about, and it’s what keeps me up staring at the ceiling until three in the morning. I am just consumed by it. Because it was my event. I was the one in charge. I’m the youth pastor, I’m the adult in the room, the one who is supposed to be shepherding these kids and keeping them safe, and I just... I failed. I failed completely. 

I keep playing that night over and over in my head, like a movie I can't turn off, just dissecting every single decision I made. I keep telling myself that if I had just ended the event earlier... I mean, why did I let it go on so long? We didn't need to be there that late. If I had just looked at my watch and said, "Alright, guys, we're wrapping up," the timing would have been entirely different. None of it would have lined up the way it did. Or... or if I had just walked him out. Why didn't I walk him out to the parking lot? It would have taken two minutes. Two minutes of my time to just walk alongside him, and I didn't do it. I was distracted. 

I should have kept better watch over those boys. That was my whole job, to watch them, to guide them, and I took my eyes off the situation. They get rowdy, they get distracted, and I knew that, but I wasn't paying close enough attention. And because of my negligence, because I didn't end things when I should have, or walk with him, or just pay attention to what those boys were doing... my cousin is gone. 

If I had just done my job, my cousin would still be here. He would still be alive. He'd still be sitting in the second pew on Sunday mornings with my aunt and uncle. And I have to look at them every week, Doctor. I have to stand up at the pulpit and look out at his parents, knowing that if I had just made one tiny different choice, their son wouldn't be dead. People in the congregation, the senior pastor, they all try to tell me, "Oh, it was a tragedy, it's not your fault, you couldn't have known." But they don't understand. They weren't the ones responsible. I was. I hold all of that weight. I just keep thinking about the exact timeline, down to the minute. If I had just said, "Let's pack it up," ten minutes sooner. Ten minutes! It’s maddening. It just eats away at me, this constant loop of "if I had just done this, if I had just done that," and the bottom line always comes back to the same awful truth: if I had been a better leader, my cousin would still be here.
Do you try to avoid feeling certain emotions when you think about that night?

Avoid feeling them? I... I do everything in my power to avoid feeling them, Doctor. Because if I actually let myself sit down and feel the full weight of it all at once, I don't think I'd ever get back up. The grief, the panic, the guilt... it's just too heavy. So, yeah, I avoid it. I mean, physically, geographically, socially... I avoid it in every possible way I can think of. 

For instance, I literally take the long way around town now every single day. I will intentionally add twenty, maybe twenty-five minutes to my drive, going all the way down the old county highway and cutting back through the far residential neighborhoods, just so I don't have to pass anywhere near the community center. Or that court. If I even see the turn-off for that street up ahead, my chest starts to get tight and I start bracing myself, so I just avoid that whole side of town entirely now. I map out my errands, my visits to congregants, everything, just to make sure I don't accidentally drive by it and trigger all those feelings I'm trying so desperately to keep shoved down. 

And it's not just the physical places, either. It's the people. You know, in a church community, people want to talk. They want to process things together, they want to offer comfort, they want to pray with you. And I know they mean well, I really do... but if somebody even starts talking about that night, if they even bring up his name or start saying things like "the Lord works in mysterious ways" about the accident, I just completely shut it down. I have to. I can't let them open that door. 

If they keep pushing, or if I feel like the conversation is even slightly steering toward what happened, I will just find a reason to leave. I'll make something up right on the spot—I'll say I need to go prep the soundboard for the worship team, or I forgot to print the youth group discussion guides, or I have a pastoral care call I'm late for. I know it probably looks incredibly rude, especially for a pastor to just abruptly walk away from someone who is trying to connect or offer sympathy, but I just can't go there with them. If I stand there and let them talk about it, the emotions just start clawing up my throat, and I can't let that happen in the middle of the church foyer. So I just run from it. I avoid the places, I avoid the conversations, I just keep moving so I don't have to actually feel it.
Do you often find yourself constantly on the lookout for potential dangers or threats, even when you're in a safe environment?

Constantly. It's... it is absolutely exhausting, Doctor. I never used to be like this, but now my brain is just always, always on high alert. Take something as simple as just sitting down in a room. I can't sit with my back to a door anymore. I just can't do it. If I go to a coffee shop, or a staff meeting, or anywhere, really, I have to be the one facing the entrance. If I can't see who is coming in, my skin just crawls, and my heart starts racing, and I can't focus on a single thing until I move my chair so I have a clear view of the room. 

And it’s even worse at church events, which is... it's terrible, because that's where I'm supposed to be present and leading. But I'm not. I'm standing there in the fellowship hall or the lobby, and someone will be talking right to me, pouring their heart out about their week or asking a question about the youth ministry, and I am completely checked out. Instead of paying attention to the people in front of me, my eyes are just darting everywhere. I’m just scanning the room, over and over. I'm watching everyone's hands, looking at what they're holding or how they're moving. I'm checking the corners of the room, looking for anything out of place. 

If we're by a window or out in the parking lot, I'm watching the street—if a car even just slows down a little bit as it drives past, my chest seizes up and I'm tracking it until it's completely gone. And exits... I literally can't walk into a room without immediately locating where the nearest exit is. I'll be nodding at a parishioner, pretending to listen, but in my head, I'm calculating exactly how to get people out of those doors if something happens. It's like I'm just waiting for the next disaster to strike, and I have to be ready this time. I have to see it coming. Even in a sanctuary, a place that is literally designed to be safe, I just feel like danger is right there, and I can't turn that radar off. Not for a single second.
Do you find yourself always being on the lookout for potential threats or dangers, even in situations where you know you are safe?

Yeah, exactly, like I was just saying... it's just this never-ending loop. Even when I know intellectually that I'm in a perfectly safe place, like the church sanctuary on a Tuesday afternoon when nobody else is even in the building, I still can't turn it off. 

Like I mentioned about the doors—it's not just a preference, it's a physical compulsion at this point. I absolutely cannot sit with my back to a door anymore. I will literally rearrange the furniture in the youth room before a meeting if I have to, just to make sure my chair is backed up against a solid wall and facing the main entrance. If I don't, the hair on the back of my neck stands up and I can't hear a word anyone is saying anyway. 

And those church events I was telling you about? It honestly breaks my heart because I'm supposed to be shepherding this flock, but I'm just... I'm not there. A parent or a kid will be standing right in front of me, pouring their heart out or asking for prayer, and I'm completely ignoring them because I'm too busy watching the hands of some guy walking into the lobby late. I'm studying the shadows in the corners of the fellowship hall. I'm staring out the glass doors, and if I see a car slowing down on the street outside, my brain instantly goes to the worst-case scenario and my chest just locks up. I'm constantly, obsessively trying to figure out where the nearest exit is and doing the math on how fast I could get everyone through it. I'm doing all of this intense threat assessment instead of actually paying attention to the people right in front of me who need their pastor. It's like my brain is permanently stuck in survival mode, and it doesn't care at all that I'm just standing at a Wednesday night potluck.
Do you believe that you are worthless or inadequate as a person because of what happened that night?

Worthless? I... no, I don't think I'd use that word. I really don't. 

I mean, given my vocation, my whole life and my entire theological framework are built around the exact opposite idea, right? I teach my youth kids every single week that every person has inherent, God-given value. So, fundamentally, at my core, I don't sit around thinking I'm just this worthless piece of garbage or that my life has absolutely no meaning anymore. I still know I'm loved, I still know I have a calling, even if I'm doing a pretty terrible job of living up to it right now with all the... the distraction and the constant scanning the room that I was just telling you about. I went through four years of undergrad really cementing my pastoral identity, and I know who I am in that regard. 

So, no, "inadequate as a person" isn't really it either. Don't get me wrong, I feel absolutely horrible about what happened. Like I said before, the guilt of it all just completely eats at me, day in and day out. I constantly replay everything, agonizing over the "what ifs" and the "if onlys," wondering how I could have changed the outcome or done something differently. But that's about my actions in that one specific situation, you know? It's about feeling the weight of that night. It doesn't make me think my entire existence is a mistake or that I'm fundamentally a bad human being. I just... I don't go down that particular mental rabbit hole. I know I still have worth, and I know my life still matters. I'm just really, really struggling to carry the weight of it all right now. But no, not worthless.

patient.answer:
Hi, doctor. Thank you. I just... I really didn't know where else to go at this point. What brings me in is that I just keep getting hit, completely out of nowhere, with this... this scene of my cousin on that pavement. It's like my brain just hijacks me. I'll be right back there, and I can hear all the shouting, the chaotic yelling from that night, and I see the lights flashing all over again. And it's so real, you know? It's not just remembering it, it's like I'm living it. 

It happens at the worst times, too. I'll just be standing there in the church office—I work in ministry, so I'm supposed to be the one holding it together for everyone else, being the steady one—and I'll be trying so hard to just act normal, to smile and do my job and be present for my congregation, but inside I'm just completely overwhelmed by the sights and sounds of that street. It just won't stop playing in my head. I can't keep pretending I'm fine when I'm constantly getting pulled back to that pavement, no matter how hard I try to just focus on my work.

inference.note: Added F43.1 due to the patient's description of intrusive memories and flashbacks of a traumatic event, which are characteristic symptoms of post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD).

I'll get home, I'll try to do my evening prayers, maybe read a few pages of a theological commentary I'm studying for my Sunday sermon, and the second my head hits the pillow, my body just completely shuts down. 

It's almost like a defense mechanism, I think. I just crash. I sleep really heavy, actually, straight through till my alarm goes off. It is honestly the only time my brain goes quiet and I get a break from the flashing lights and the yelling. So, no, I haven't had any trouble sleeping. The nights aren't the problem for me... it's the waking hours that are the nightmare. People would come to me because I was calm, because I was the safe harbor when things got heated.

But lately... it's like my fuse is just completely gone. It's like it burned away the night my cousin died, and now there's just a raw wire right under my skin. Just last week, we had our monthly deacons meeting. And it's usually just mundane stuff—budget approvals, planning the church picnic, scheduling volunteers for the food pantry. Normal, boring church business. And one of the older deacons, a man I have known and respected since I started this job, he just asked a simple question about the youth group budget. He wasn't being malicious or critical, he just asked if we could maybe trim a few dollars from the pizza fund. 

And doctor, I just... I snapped. I completely lost it. It wasn't just a mild disagreement; I raised my voice. I was practically yelling at him, right there in the fellowship hall in front of everyone. I was talking to him like he was the enemy, like he was actively trying to sabotage the entire ministry, over fifty dollars in pizza money. I could see the shock on everyone's faces. The room went dead silent. And it's not just the deacons, either. I've been doing it with the youth leaders too, the volunteers who give up their Wednesday nights to help me. If they are five minutes late, or if they forget to print the discussion questions, I just lash out. 

And the worst part... the absolute worst part is how I feel afterward. The second the words are out of my mouth, the second I see them shrink back, I just feel this crushing wave of guilt. I hate it. I hate how fast I go from zero to absolute rage. I hate that I'm hurting the people who are trying to support me, the people I'm supposed to be leading. I'll go back to my office and just put my head on my desk and think, 'Who am I becoming?' It's like I have all this jagged, chaotic energy trapped inside me from that pavement, and it just explodes out of me at the people who least deserve it. I have to spend half my week apologizing for things I said in the heat of the moment, and I just... I don't know how to stop it from happening. It's like I'm not even in control of my own reactions anymore.

Outside my body... no. No, I don't think I've ever felt that. Honestly, it's almost the exact opposite for me. If anything, I feel entirely too trapped inside my body when it happens, if that makes sense. 

I know some people talk about feeling like they're floating or like they're watching a movie of their own life when things get to be too much... we actually touched on that a little bit in some of my pastoral counseling courses in undergrad, how the mind sometimes tries to protect itself by just detaching from reality when the pain is too heavy. And to be completely honest with you, Doctor, there are times when I almost wish my brain would do that. I wish I could just check out and watch from the ceiling for a few minutes just to get a break from the sheer intensity of it all. 

But for me, when the memories come crashing in, or when I get so overwhelmed by the grief and the panic that I can barely breathe, I am painfully aware of my physical body. I feel every single thing. My chest gets incredibly tight, my hands start sweating, my heart feels like it's going to hammer right through my ribs. I'm not watching myself from above; I'm right there, anchored to the ground, feeling like the weight of the entire sanctuary is pressing down on my shoulders. 

Like, just the other day, I was standing in the church foyer talking to one of our elderly members about the Sunday flower arrangements, and I heard a car backfire out on the main street. And instantly, I wasn't floating away. I was right back on that pavement. I could practically feel the cold concrete under my knees again, I could smell the exhaust in the air. I gripped the edge of the wooden welcome table so hard my knuckles went completely white, just trying to stay upright and keep my balance. I was so hyper-aware of my own physical panic, just praying she wouldn't notice that my hands were shaking and I was struggling to pull air into my lungs. So, no... I don't ever get that feeling of watching myself from the outside. I am stuck right inside every single agonizing second of it, and it feels like there is absolutely no escape.

A bad person? ...No. No, I don't think I would say that. I mean, I know I just went on and on about the guilt and the shame, and feeling like a massive failure, but... there is a difference, I think, between failing and being fundamentally bad. I don't believe I'm a bad person.

My intentions have never been malicious. I never wanted anyone to get hurt, ever. So, when I really sit down and examine my heart—which is something we’re taught to do constantly in seminary, just this rigorous spiritual self-examination—I don't find evil there. It's like I'm hyper-connected to my own skin, and it's just constantly buzzing with all this tension. I look at the people around me—the congregation, the kids, the senior pastor—and they all feel very, very real. The conversations we have are real. I might feel like there's this invisible barrier between me and them sometimes, but that's not because I'm disconnected from reality. It's just because I'm carrying this massive, suffocating weight of guilt that they don't see or fully understand. But I am definitely, one hundred percent in my own body. 

I feel every physical ache, every time my stomach ties itself into knots—which is basically constantly these days. It's just... I don't know how else to describe it, Doctor, except that none of it feels alive in me anymore. patient.answer:
Do I blame myself? I mean... how could I not? Honestly, Doctor, that is... that is the absolute core of it all. It’s what I wake up thinking about, and it’s what keeps me up staring at the ceiling until three in the morning. I am just consumed by it. Because it was my event. I was the one in charge. I’m the youth pastor, I’m the adult in the room, the one who is supposed to be shepherding these kids and keeping them safe, and I just... I failed. I failed completely. 

I keep playing that night over and over in my head, like a movie I can't turn off, just dissecting every single decision I made. I keep telling myself that if I had just ended the event earlier... I mean, why did I let it go on so long? We didn't need to be there that late. If I had just looked at my watch and said, "Alright, guys, we're wrapping up," the timing would have been entirely different. None of it would have lined up the way it did. Or... or if I had just walked him out. Why didn't I walk him out to the parking lot? It would have taken two minutes. Two minutes of my time to just walk alongside him, and I didn't do it. I was distracted. 

I should have kept better watch over those boys. That was my whole job, to watch them, to guide them, and I took my eyes off the situation. They get rowdy, they get distracted, and I knew that, but I wasn't paying close enough attention. And because of my negligence, because I didn't end things when I should have, or walk with him, or just pay attention to what those boys were doing... my cousin is gone. 

If I had just done my job, my cousin would still be here. He would still be alive. He'd still be sitting in the second pew on Sunday mornings with my aunt and uncle. And I have to look at them every week, Doctor. I have to stand up at the pulpit and look out at his parents, knowing that if I had just made one tiny different choice, their son wouldn't be dead. People in the congregation, the senior pastor, they all try to tell me, "Oh, it was a tragedy, it's not your fault, you couldn't have known." But they don't understand. They weren't the ones responsible. I was. I hold all of that weight. I just keep thinking about the exact timeline, down to the minute. If I had just said, "Let's pack it up," ten minutes sooner. Ten minutes! It’s maddening. It just eats away at me, this constant loop of "if I had just done this, if I had just done that," and the bottom line always comes back to the same awful truth: if I had been a better leader, my cousin would still be here.

Instead of paying attention to the people in front of me, my eyes are just darting everywhere. I’m just scanning the room, over and over. I'm watching everyone's hands, looking at what they're holding or how they're moving. I'm checking the corners of the room, looking for anything out of place. 

If we're by a window or out in the parking lot, I'm watching the street—if a car even just slows down a little bit as it drives past, my chest seizes up and I'm tracking it until it's completely gone. And exits... I literally can't walk into a room without immediately locating where the nearest exit is. I'll be nodding at a parishioner, pretending to listen, but in my head, I'm calculating exactly how to get people out of those doors if something happens. It's like I'm just waiting for the next disaster to strike, and I have to be ready this time. I have to see it coming. Even in a sanctuary, a place that is literally designed to be safe, I just feel like danger is right there, and I can't turn that radar off. Not for a single second.

doctor.question: Do you find yourself always being on the lookout for potential threats or dangers, even in situations where you know you are safe?

target_item.name: Hypervigilance
target_item.manifestation: I can't sit with my back to a door anymore, and at church events I'm always watching hands, corners, cars slowing down, and where the nearest exit is instead of paying attention to the people in front of me.
target_item.reason: The doctor is repeating the question about being on the lookout for potential threats or dangers, which directly assesses for hypervigilance.

patient.answer:
Yeah, exactly, like I was just saying... it's just this never-ending loop. Even when I know intellectually that I'm in a perfectly safe place, like the church sanctuary on a Tuesday afternoon when nobody else is even in the building, I still can't turn it off. 

Like I mentioned about the doors—it's not just a preference, it's a physical compulsion at this point. I absolutely cannot sit with my back to a door anymore. I will literally rearrange the furniture in the youth room before a meeting if I have to, just to make sure my chair is backed up against a solid wall and facing the main entrance. If I don't, the hair on the back of my neck stands up and I can't hear a word anyone is saying anyway. 

And those church events I was telling you about? It honestly breaks my heart because I'm supposed to be shepherding this flock, but I'm just... I'm not there. A parent or a kid will be standing right in front of me, pouring their heart out or asking for prayer, and I'm completely ignoring them because I'm too busy watching the hands of some guy walking into the lobby late. I'm studying the shadows in the corners of the fellowship hall. I'm staring out the glass doors, and if I see a car slowing down on the street outside, my brain instantly goes to the worst-case scenario and my chest just locks up. I'm constantly, obsessively trying to figure out where the nearest exit is and doing the math on how fast I could get everyone through it. I'm doing all of this intense threat assessment instead of actually paying attention to the people right in front of me who need their pastor. It's like my brain is permanently stuck in survival mode, and it doesn't care at all that I'm just standing at a Wednesday night potluck.

doctor.intent: Determine the presence of persistent negative beliefs about oneself
doctor.question: Do you believe that you are worthless or inadequate as a person because of what happened that night?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about persistent negative beliefs about oneself (e.g., feeling worthless or inadequate), which corresponds to a distinct PTSD symptom that is not included in the patient's symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Worthless? I... no, I don't think I'd use that word. I really don't. 

I mean, given my vocation, my whole life and my entire theological framework are built around the exact opposite idea, right? I teach my youth kids every single week that every person has inherent, God-given value. So, fundamentally, at my core, I don't sit around thinking I'm just this worthless piece of garbage or that my life has absolutely no meaning anymore. I still know I'm loved, I still know I have a calling, even if I'm doing a pretty terrible job of living up to it right now with all the... the distraction and the constant scanning the room that I was just telling you about. I went through four years of undergrad really cementing my pastoral identity, and I know who I am in that regard. 

So, no, "inadequate as a person" isn't really it either. Don't get me wrong, I feel absolutely horrible about what happened. Like I said before, the guilt of it all just completely eats at me, day in and day out. I constantly replay everything, agonizing over the "what ifs" and the "if onlys," wondering how I could have changed the outcome or done something differently. But that's about my actions in that one specific situation, you know? It's about feeling the weight of that night. It doesn't make me think my entire existence is a mistake or that I'm fundamentally a bad human being. I just... I don't go down that particular mental rabbit hole. I know I still have worth, and I know my life still matters. I'm just really, really struggling to carry the weight of it all right now. But no, not worthless.
